title: Waaqa and the First Rain
summary: When the sky was still close to the earth, a woman’s pestle struck it, and Waaqa withdrew — but left the rain as a gift.
moral: Do not strike at the sky; ask it for water instead.
attribution: A traditional Oromo tale, retold for Ubuntu Tales.

cover.alt: Blue-grey rain falling in long lines from flat clouds onto a green sprout and distant peaks

sentences.text: The Oromo say that in the beginning Waaqa placed the sky very near the earth, so near that a tall person could touch it with a stick.
The sky was warm and generous, and it kept the earth from growing cold at night.
The people lived well beneath it.
They had cattle and grain and enough water.
The trouble began when a woman was pounding grain in her mortar with a long wooden pestle, and the sky was hanging low above her head.
She lifted the pestle high and struck the sky by accident.
There was a sound like thunder, and the sky shuddered and began to rise.
The woman dropped her pestle and held up her hands.
“I did not mean it,” she cried.
Waaqa rose a little, and the earth grew cooler.
Waaqa rose a little more, and the people could no longer reach up and touch it.
The woman wept, because she had undone a kindness with one careless blow.
But Waaqa did not leave the earth without help.
“Since I can no longer be near you,” Waaqa said, “I will send my water down.
Ask for it with your fields and your herds, and with a clean heart.
I will hear you from higher up.”
And that is why the rain comes from a sky that no hand can reach, and why the old people say you should not strike at the sky in anger or in carelessness.
Ask, and be ready to be answered.
The woman’s pestle is still in the story, and the rain is still the answer.
